The term $(\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c})$ produces a purely scalar quantity, and the cross product operation ($\times$) is exclusively defined between two vectors. This renders the entire expression mathematically meaningless. Always double-check that your cross products are strictly linking two vector quantities.

Properties of the Scalar Triple Product.concept: Properties of the Scalar Triple Product (Cyclic Permutation and Operator Interchange)
Properties of the Scalar Triple Product.content:
Consider a scenario where you are given three non-zero vectors, $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$, which form a parallelepiped of volume $25$ cubic units. 
1. If we construct a new vector $\mathbf{D}$ defined simply as $\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}$, what happens to the scalar triple product $[\mathbf{D}\ \mathbf{B}\ \mathbf{C}]$? 
2. Try expanding this using the distributive property of the dot and cross products. You will obtain $[\mathbf{A}\ \mathbf{B}\ \mathbf{C}] + [\mathbf{B}\ \mathbf{B}\ \mathbf{C}]$. 
3. Why must the second term, $[\mathbf{B}\ \mathbf{B}\ \mathbf{C}]$, be exactly zero from both an algebraic perspective (evaluating the cross product) and a geometric perspective (analyzing the volume of a parallelepiped with two identical edge vectors)? 
4. Extending this logic, if you smoothly animate vector $\mathbf{A}$ in three-dimensional space such that it slowly collapses into the plane defined by $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$, how does the value of the scalar triple product continuously evolve, and what specific physical dimension of the parallelepiped is driving this mathematical limit towards zero?

Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant C.concept: Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant Conditions (Standard and General Basis)
Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant C.content:
The concept of coplanarity asks a deeply fundamental geometric question: do three given vectors lie flat within the exact same two-dimensional plane? If we place their tails at a common origin, do they fail to construct any genuine three-dimensional depth? 

We know that the Scalar Triple Product measures the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by three vectors. Naturally, if the vectors are entirely locked within a single 2D plane, they possess zero 'height' out of that plane. Consequently, the 3D volume they span is utterly crushed to zero. Therefore, three vectors are explicitly coplanar if and only if their Scalar Triple Product equals zero.

However, in JEE Advanced coordinate geometry, we rarely deal with vectors purely as abstract arrows. We represent them algebraically as linear combinations of a foundational set of basis vectors. Most commonly, this is the standard orthogonal basis $(\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k})$. When we express our three target vectors using components in this basis, determining their coplanarity translates into an elegant matrix operation. We extract the scalar components, stack them into a $3 \times 3$ matrix, and calculate its determinant. The determinant acts as a master scaling factor for volume. If the vectors are coplanar, the algebraic determinant of their components collapses to exactly zero.

The profound extension of this rule—which is frequently exploited in advanced exam questions—is that this determinant condition is completely independent of the standard orthogonal basis! As long as you have any three arbitrary basis vectors $(\boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma})$ that form a valid, non-coplanar 3D framework, you can test the coplanarity of your derived vectors simply by evaluating the determinant of their scalar coefficients. This highlights the beautiful intersection between vector geometry and linear algebra: setting the determinant of coefficients to zero is functionally identical to proving that one vector can be expressed as a perfect linear combination of the other two.

Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant C.concept: Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant Conditions (Standard and General Basis)
Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant C.content:
The algebraic test for the coplanarity of three vectors expressed as linear combinations is formalized through the following definitive theorem involving determinants.

**General Basis Coplanarity Theorem**
Let $\boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\beta},$ and $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ be any three strictly non-coplanar vectors (thereby acting as a valid basis for $\mathbb{R}^3$). Let three new vectors $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}$ be constructed as linear combinations of this basis:
$\mathbf{a} = a_1\boldsymbol{\alpha} + a_2\boldsymbol{\beta} + a_3\boldsymbol{\gamma}$
$\mathbf{b} = b_1\boldsymbol{\alpha} + b_2\boldsymbol{\beta} + b_3\boldsymbol{\gamma}$
$\mathbf{c} = c_1\boldsymbol{\alpha} + c_2\boldsymbol{\beta} + c_3\boldsymbol{\gamma}$

The vectors $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}$ are coplanar **if and only if** the determinant of their scalar coefficients evaluates to exactly zero:
$$ \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0 $$

**Standard Basis Corollary**
If we explicitly replace the general basis vectors $\boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}$ with the standard, mutually orthogonal unit vectors $\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}$, the rule simplifies to the most commonly utilized form in 3D geometry. For vectors $\mathbf{a} = a_1\mathbf{i} + a_2\mathbf{j} + a_3\mathbf{k}$, $\mathbf{b} = b_1\mathbf{i} + b_2\mathbf{j} + b_3\mathbf{k}$, and $\mathbf{c} = c_1\mathbf{i} + c_2\mathbf{j} + c_3\mathbf{k}$, they are coplanar if and only if:
$$ \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0 $$

*Crucial Condition:* The biconditional ('if and only if') nature of this theorem implies it works flawlessly in both directions. If you know the determinant is zero, the vectors are definitively coplanar. If you are told the vectors are coplanar, you have the mathematical authority to immediately set their coefficient determinant to zero to solve for an unknown variable.

Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant C.concept: Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant Conditions (Standard and General Basis)
Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant C.content:
Let's meticulously derive the general basis coplanarity theorem. This proof demonstrates the power of the distributive properties of dot and cross products.

We start by evaluating the Scalar Triple Product of the derived vectors: $[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}] = \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})$.
Substitute the linear combinations:
$\mathbf{a} \cdot [ (b_1\boldsymbol{\alpha} + b_2\boldsymbol{\beta} + b_3\boldsymbol{\gamma}) \times (c_1\boldsymbol{\alpha} + c_2\boldsymbol{\beta} + c_3\boldsymbol{\gamma}) ]$

When we expand the cross product $(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})$ distributively, we obtain nine terms. However, terms involving the cross product of a basis vector with itself (like $\boldsymbol{\alpha} \times \boldsymbol{\alpha}$) immediately collapse to the zero vector $\mathbf{0}$. The remaining six non-zero terms can be grouped by factoring out their scalar coefficients. Using the anti-commutative property (e.g., $\boldsymbol{\beta} \times \boldsymbol{\alpha} = -\boldsymbol{\alpha} \times \boldsymbol{\beta}$), we consolidate the terms into three groups:
$\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} = (b_2 c_3 - b_3 c_2)(\boldsymbol{\beta} \times \boldsymbol{\gamma}) + (b_3 c_1 - b_1 c_3)(\boldsymbol{\gamma} \times \boldsymbol{\alpha}) + (b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1)(\boldsymbol{\alpha} \times \boldsymbol{\beta})$

Next, we take the dot product of $\mathbf{a} = a_1\boldsymbol{\alpha} + a_2\boldsymbol{\beta} + a_3\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ with this massive resulting vector. 
When we systematically distribute the dot product, any term where a basis vector is dotted with a cross product containing that same vector (e.g., $\boldsymbol{\alpha} \cdot (\boldsymbol{\alpha} \times \boldsymbol{\beta})$) maps to zero, because $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ is geometrically perpendicular to the vector resulting from $(\boldsymbol{\alpha} \times \boldsymbol{\beta})$. The only surviving terms are those that pair up all three distinct basis vectors. 

This leaves us with:
$= a_1(b_2 c_3 - b_3 c_2)[\boldsymbol{\alpha}\ \boldsymbol{\beta}\ \boldsymbol{\gamma}] + a_2(b_3 c_1 - b_1 c_3)[\boldsymbol{\beta}\ \boldsymbol{\gamma}\ \boldsymbol{\alpha}] + a_3(b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1)[\boldsymbol{\gamma}\ \boldsymbol{\alpha}\ \boldsymbol{\beta}]$

Using our knowledge of cyclic permutations, we know $[\boldsymbol{\beta}\ \boldsymbol{\gamma}\ \boldsymbol{\alpha}] = [\boldsymbol{\gamma}\ \boldsymbol{\alpha}\ \boldsymbol{\beta}] = [\boldsymbol{\alpha}\ \boldsymbol{\beta}\ \boldsymbol{\gamma}]$. We can neatly factor out this fundamental scalar triple product:
$[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}] = \{ a_1(b_2 c_3 - b_3 c_2) - a_2(b_1 c_3 - b_3 c_1) + a_3(b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1) \} [\boldsymbol{\alpha}\ \boldsymbol{\beta}\ \boldsymbol{\gamma}]$

Examine the scalar expression inside the curly braces. It is precisely the first-row cofactor expansion of a $3 \times 3$ determinant! Therefore:
$[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}] = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} [\boldsymbol{\alpha}\ \boldsymbol{\beta}\ \boldsymbol{\gamma}]$

We are given that $\boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}$ are non-coplanar, which mathematically guarantees that their scalar triple product $[\boldsymbol{\alpha}\ \boldsymbol{\beta}\ \boldsymbol{\gamma}] \neq 0$. Therefore, the only way for the derived vectors $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ to be coplanar (meaning $[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}] = 0$) is if the determinant of their coefficients is strictly equal to zero. The derivation is completely solid.

Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant C.concept: Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant Conditions (Standard and General Basis)
Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant C.content:
**Problem Statement:**
Determine the exact value of the scalar parameter $\lambda$ for which the three vectors $\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$, $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}$, and $\mathbf{c} = 3\mathbf{i} + \lambda\mathbf{j} + 5\mathbf{k}$ are perfectly coplanar.

**Strategy:**
Since we are operating within the standard orthogonal basis $(\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k})$, the coplanarity constraint demands that the Scalar Triple Product $[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}]$ must equate to zero. We will construct a $3 \times 3$ determinant utilizing the scalar components of each vector as the respective rows, set the entire determinant equal to zero, and perform basic algebraic expansion to isolate and solve for $\lambda$.

**Step-by-Step Algebraic Solution:**
1. Form the coefficient matrix determinant and enforce the zero condition:
$$ \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & \lambda & 5 \end{vmatrix} = 0 $$

2. Expand the determinant meticulously along the first row. Pay strict attention to the alternating sign pattern $(+, -, +)$:
$$ 2 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ \lambda & 5 \end{vmatrix} - (-1) \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{vmatrix} + 1 \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0 $$

3. Calculate the $2 \times 2$ minor determinants:
   - Minor 1: $(2)(5) - (-3)(\lambda) = 10 + 3\lambda$
   - Minor 2: $(1)(5) - (-3)(3) = 5 + 9 = 14$
   - Minor 3: $(1)(\lambda) - (2)(3) = \lambda - 6$

4. Substitute these minors back into the expanded equation:
$$ 2(10 + 3\lambda) + 1(14) + 1(\lambda - 6) = 0 $$

5. Distribute and consolidate all like terms:
$$ 20 + 6\lambda + 14 + \lambda - 6 = 0 $$
$$ 7\lambda + 28 = 0 $$
$$ 7\lambda = -28 $$
$$ \lambda = -4 $$

**Final Answer Verification:**
The value is $\lambda = -4$. To rigorously verify this without relying solely on the determinant, we test for linear dependence. Can we express $\mathbf{c}$ as $x\mathbf{a} + y\mathbf{b}$? 
We set up the component equations:
$2x + y = 3$ (from the $\mathbf{i}$ component)
$-x + 2y = -4$ (from the $\mathbf{j}$ component)
$x - 3y = 5$ (from the $\mathbf{k}$ component)

Multiplying the second equation by 2 gives $-2x + 4y = -8$. Adding this to the first equation yields $5y = -5$, meaning $y = -1$. Substituting $y = -1$ into the first equation yields $2x - 1 = 3$, meaning $x = 2$. 
Finally, we check these values against the third equation: $(2) - 3(-1) = 2 + 3 = 5$. This matches the $\mathbf{k}$ component perfectly! The vector $\mathbf{c}$ is explicitly proven to be a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ (specifically $\mathbf{c} = 2\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}$), absolutely guaranteeing their geometric coplanarity.

Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant C.concept: Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant Conditions (Standard and General Basis)
Coplanarity of Vectors and Determinant C.content:
A highly insidious trap in advanced vector problems involves completely forgetting the implicit prerequisites of Corollary 6.17 regarding a general set of basis vectors. 

Imagine an exam question that defines $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ in terms of three generic vectors $\boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}$. A student might immediately slam the coefficients into a determinant, find that the determinant evaluates to $15$ (non-zero), and confidently declare that $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ are non-coplanar. 

However, what if the problem subtly stated earlier that $\boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}$ themselves lie in the same plane? If the foundational basis vectors are already coplanar, their own scalar triple product is identically zero ($[\boldsymbol{\alpha}\ \boldsymbol{\beta}\ \boldsymbol{\gamma}] = 0$). Returning to our derived equation: $[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}] = (\text{Determinant}) \times [\boldsymbol{\alpha}\ \boldsymbol{\beta}\ \boldsymbol{\gamma}]$. If the basis STP is zero, then $[\mathbf{a}\ \mathbf{b}\ \mathbf{c}]$ will absolutely evaluate to zero regardless of what the matrix determinant calculates to! 

Therefore, any linear combinations constructed from a coplanar basis are automatically and inescapably coplanar. Calculating the matrix determinant in this context is completely meaningless. You must always confirm that the underlying framework $(\boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma})$ spans full 3D space before utilizing the matrix determinant shortcut as a definitive test for coplanarity.

Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary No.concept: Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary Non-Coplanar Basis
Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary No.content:
To deeply understand how vectors behave, we must first divorce the idea of a vector from the standard Cartesian coordinate system. Most students are incredibly comfortable with the orthonormal basis consisting of the unit vectors $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, and $\hat{k}$. In this standard world, calculating the scalar triple product (which geometrically represents the signed volume of a parallelepiped formed by three vectors) is as simple as taking the determinant of their scalar components. But what happens if we skew our universe? 

Imagine a world where the fundamental building blocks—our basis vectors—are not mutually perpendicular, nor are they of unit length. Let us call these arbitrary basis vectors $\vec{\alpha}$, $\vec{\beta}$, and $\vec{\gamma}$. As long as these three vectors do not lie in the same plane (meaning they are non-coplanar, and their own scalar triple product $[\vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma}]$ is non-zero), they can span the entire three-dimensional space. Any arbitrary vectors $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, and $\vec{c}$ can be expressed as unique linear combinations of $\vec{\alpha}$, $\vec{\beta}$, and $\vec{\gamma}$. 

Now, if we want to find the volume of the parallelepiped formed by $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, and $\vec{c}$, how does the skewness of our underlying coordinate system affect the result? The beautiful truth of linear algebra is that the volume scales linearly. The determinant of the coefficients of $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, and $\vec{c}$ (when expressed in the $\vec{\alpha}$, $\vec{\beta}$, $\vec{\gamma}$ basis) merely tells us the 'relative volume'—the volume of the new parallelepiped relative to the fundamental building block. 

To find the true, absolute volume in standard space, we must multiply this relative volume (the determinant of the components) by the volume of the fundamental building block itself, which is the scalar triple product $[\vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma}]$. This concept acts as a bridge between abstract vector spaces and measurable geometric quantities, revealing that determinants are essentially volume-scaling factors under linear transformations. If the fundamental building blocks flatten out (become coplanar), their volume becomes zero, and consequently, the volume of any structure built upon them also collapses to absolute zero, regardless of the coordinate coefficients.

Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary No.concept: Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary Non-Coplanar Basis
Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary No.content:
Let $\vec{\alpha}$, $\vec{\beta}$, and $\vec{\gamma}$ be three non-coplanar basis vectors in a three-dimensional space, meaning their scalar triple product satisfies $[\vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma}] \neq 0$.

Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, and $\vec{c}$ be any three arbitrary vectors expressed as linear combinations of this given basis such that:
$\vec{a} = a_1\vec{\alpha} + a_2\vec{\beta} + a_3\vec{\gamma}$
$\vec{b} = b_1\vec{\alpha} + b_2\vec{\beta} + b_3\vec{\gamma}$
$\vec{c} = c_1\vec{\alpha} + c_2\vec{\beta} + c_3\vec{\gamma}$

Then, the scalar triple product of the vectors $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, and $\vec{c}$ is given by the theorem:

$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} [\vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma}]$

Conditions and Constraints:
1. The coefficients $a_i, b_i, c_i$ must be real scalars.
2. If the basis vectors $\vec{\alpha}$, $\vec{\beta}$, $\vec{\gamma}$ are coplanar, then $[\vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma}] = 0$, forcing the entire scalar triple product $[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]$ to evaluate to zero, which makes sense geometrically since vectors defined entirely within a 2D plane cannot form a 3D volume.
3. If $\vec{\alpha} = \hat{i}$, $\vec{\beta} = \hat{j}$, and $\vec{\gamma} = \hat{k}$, then $[\hat{i} \, \hat{j} \, \hat{k}] = 1$, and the formula neatly collapses back to the standard determinant representation.

Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary No.concept: Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary Non-Coplanar Basis
Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary No.content:
Let us rigorously derive the expression for the scalar triple product in an arbitrary basis, ensuring no algebraic nuances are overlooked.

We start with the definitions:
$\vec{a} = a_1\vec{\alpha} + a_2\vec{\beta} + a_3\vec{\gamma}$
$\vec{b} = b_1\vec{\alpha} + b_2\vec{\beta} + b_3\vec{\gamma}$
$\vec{c} = c_1\vec{\alpha} + c_2\vec{\beta} + c_3\vec{\gamma}$

The scalar triple product is defined as $[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$.

Step 1: Expand the cross product $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$.
By substituting the linear combinations, we get:
$\vec{b} \times \vec{c} = (b_1\vec{\alpha} + b_2\vec{\beta} + b_3\vec{\gamma}) \times (c_1\vec{\alpha} + c_2\vec{\beta} + c_3\vec{\gamma})$

Because the vector cross product is distributive over addition, we expand this into 9 terms. However, we immediately apply the self-annihilation property of the cross product: $\vec{v} \times \vec{v} = \vec{0}$. Thus, terms like $\vec{\alpha} \times \vec{\alpha}$, $\vec{\beta} \times \vec{\beta}$, and $\vec{\gamma} \times \vec{\gamma}$ vanish.

We group the surviving terms by utilizing the anti-commutative property $\vec{v} \times \vec{w} = -(\vec{w} \times \vec{v})$:
$\vec{b} \times \vec{c} = (b_2c_3 - b_3c_2)(\vec{\beta} \times \vec{\gamma}) + (b_3c_1 - b_1c_3)(\vec{\gamma} \times \vec{\alpha}) + (b_1c_2 - b_2c_1)(\vec{\alpha} \times \vec{\beta})$

Notice that the scalar coefficients here are exactly the $2 \times 2$ minor determinants from the second and third rows of our target $3 \times 3$ determinant matrix!

Step 2: Perform the dot product with $\vec{a}$.
Now, we evaluate $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$.
Substitute $\vec{a} = a_1\vec{\alpha} + a_2\vec{\beta} + a_3\vec{\gamma}$ into the expression:
$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = (a_1\vec{\alpha} + a_2\vec{\beta} + a_3\vec{\gamma}) \cdot \left[ (b_2c_3 - b_3c_2)(\vec{\beta} \times \vec{\gamma}) + \dots \right]$

Again, we distribute the dot product. This generates 9 scalar triple product terms of the basis vectors. Crucially, any scalar triple product containing a repeated vector is identically zero (e.g., $\vec{\alpha} \cdot (\vec{\gamma} \times \vec{\alpha}) = 0$).

The only terms that survive are the permutations of all three distinct vectors:
Term 1: $a_1(b_2c_3 - b_3c_2) [\vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma}]$
Term 2: $a_2(b_3c_1 - b_1c_3) [\vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma} \, \vec{\alpha}]$
Term 3: $a_3(b_1c_2 - b_2c_1) [\vec{\gamma} \, \vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta}]$

Step 3: Cyclic properties of the Scalar Triple Product.
Recall that cyclic permutations of a scalar triple product preserve its value:
$[\vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma} \, \vec{\alpha}] = [\vec{\gamma} \, \vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta}] = [\vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma}]$

Substituting this equivalence, we can factor out $[\vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma}]$:
$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \left( a_1(b_2c_3 - b_3c_2) - a_2(b_1c_3 - b_3c_1) + a_3(b_1c_2 - b_2c_1) \right) [\vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma}]$

Step 4: Final Determinant Form.
The algebraic expression inside the parenthesis is exactly the cofactor expansion along the first row of a $3 \times 3$ determinant. Therefore, we arrive at our final result:
$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} [\vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma}]$. 
This completes the derivation.

Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary No.concept: Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary Non-Coplanar Basis
Scalar Triple Product in an Arbitrary No.content:
A very common and highly penalized trap in JEE Advanced occurs when examiners present a set of basis vectors that look deceptively simple but are NOT orthonormal. 

For instance, an examiner might give vectors $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ in terms of vectors $\vec{u}, \vec{v}, \vec{w}$, where $\vec{u}, \vec{v}, \vec{w}$ have lengths 2, 3, and 4 respectively, and have specific angles between them. A student in a rush will extract the coefficient matrix, calculate the determinant, and present that as the final answer for $[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]$. 

Algebraic reason for the mistake: The student implicitly assumed that $[\vec{u} \, \vec{v} \, \vec{w}] = 1$. The determinant of coefficients ONLY gives you the volume ratio relative to the basis. If the basis is not standard $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$, you are strictly forbidden from ignoring the trailing $[\vec{\alpha} \, \vec{\beta} \, \vec{\gamma}]$ multiplier. Always explicitly write out the full formula to avoid leaving behind the fundamental volume unit.

Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (G.concept: Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (Gramian-like Determinant)
Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (G.content:
To appreciate the product of two scalar triple products, we must view it through the lens of analytical geometry and linear algebra. The scalar triple product, $[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]$, encodes the signed volume of a parallelepiped. But computationally, it relies on cross products, which are notoriously tied to the specific three-dimensional coordinate axes we use. Cross products yield vectors, and dealing with vector operators inside complex equations can become analytically cumbersome.

What happens when we multiply two volumes together? For example, multiplying $[\vec{l} \, \vec{m} \, \vec{n}]$ with $[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]$? The resulting mathematical structure is profound. By utilizing the properties of determinant multiplication, we can completely eliminate cross products from the expression. We can transform a product of volumes into a pure determinant consisting strictly of dot products (inner products) between the individual vectors.

Why is this transformation practically magical? Because dot products only depend on lengths and angles—they are absolute invariants. They do not care about how the coordinate axes are oriented. If an examiner gives you the lengths of 6 vectors and the angles between them, but gives you zero information about their $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ components, calculating their scalar triple products directly is impossible. However, by using this determinant identity, you bypass the need for coordinate systems entirely. This converts a 3D geometry problem into a pure trigonometric and scalar matrix problem. This determinant form is deeply related to the Gramian matrix, which measures the linear independence and spanned volume of a set of vectors using only their mutual inner products.

Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (G.concept: Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (Gramian-like Determinant)
Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (G.content:
Let $\vec{l}, \vec{m}, \vec{n}$ and $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ be any two sets of vectors in three-dimensional space.

The product of their scalar triple products can be expressed purely in terms of dot products (scalar products) as the determinant of a $3 \times 3$ matrix:

$[\vec{l} \, \vec{m} \, \vec{n}] \times [\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \begin{vmatrix} \vec{l} \cdot \vec{a} & \vec{l} \cdot \vec{b} & \vec{l} \cdot \vec{c} \\ \vec{m} \cdot \vec{a} & \vec{m} \cdot \vec{b} & \vec{m} \cdot \vec{c} \\ \vec{n} \cdot \vec{a} & \vec{n} \cdot \vec{b} & \vec{n} \cdot \vec{c} \end{vmatrix}$

Conditions and Constraints:
1. All vectors must exist in a valid three-dimensional Euclidean space (where the cross product is well-defined).
2. The resulting matrix element at row $i$, column $j$ is the dot product of the $i$-th vector of the first set and the $j$-th vector of the second set.
3. A special corollary arises when the two sets of vectors are identical (i.e., $\vec{l}=\vec{a}$, $\vec{m}=\vec{b}$, $\vec{n}=\vec{c}$). In this case, the square of the scalar triple product is equal to its Gramian determinant:
$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]^2 = \begin{vmatrix} \vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} & \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} & \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} \\ \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a} & \vec{b} \cdot \vec{b} & \vec{b} \cdot \vec{c} \\ \vec{c} \cdot \vec{a} & \vec{c} \cdot \vec{b} & \vec{c} \cdot \vec{c} \end{vmatrix}$

Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (G.concept: Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (Gramian-like Determinant)
Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (G.content:
The derivation relies fundamentally on expressing the scalar triple product as a determinant in a standard Cartesian basis and applying the rule for the multiplication of two determinants.

Let the vectors be resolved into their $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ components:
$\vec{l} = l_1\hat{i} + l_2\hat{j} + l_3\hat{k}$
$\vec{m} = m_1\hat{i} + m_2\hat{j} + m_3\hat{k}$
$\vec{n} = n_1\hat{i} + n_2\hat{j} + n_3\hat{k}$

Similarly, let the components for the second set be $a_i, b_i, c_i$.

Step 1: Write the STPs as determinants.
$[\vec{l} \, \vec{m} \, \vec{n}] = \begin{vmatrix} l_1 & l_2 & l_3 \\ m_1 & m_2 & m_3 \\ n_1 & n_2 & n_3 \end{vmatrix}$

$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \\ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}$

Step 2: Employ the Matrix Transpose Property.
We know that the determinant of a matrix is equal to the determinant of its transpose. Therefore, we can transpose the second determinant without altering its value:
$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}$

Step 3: Multiply the two determinants using Matrix Multiplication (Row-by-Column).
Now we multiply the two matrices. Let matrix $P$ be the first matrix and $Q^T$ be the transposed second matrix. We compute the determinant of $P \times Q^T$.

The element in the 1st row and 1st column of the product matrix is the dot product of the 1st row of $P$ and the 1st column of $Q^T$:
Element_{11} = $l_1a_1 + l_2a_2 + l_3a_3$. 
Notice that this algebraic sum is exactly the definition of the dot product $\vec{l} \cdot \vec{a}$!

Similarly, the element in the 1st row and 2nd column is:
Element_{12} = $l_1b_1 + l_2b_2 + l_3b_3 = \vec{l} \cdot \vec{b}$.

Step 4: Construct the final determinant.
Extrapolating this row-by-column multiplication across all 9 elements, we populate the entire $3 \times 3$ determinant matrix purely with dot products:

$\det(P \times Q^T) = \begin{vmatrix} \vec{l} \cdot \vec{a} & \vec{l} \cdot \vec{b} & \vec{l} \cdot \vec{c} \\ \vec{m} \cdot \vec{a} & \vec{m} \cdot \vec{b} & \vec{m} \cdot \vec{c} \\ \vec{n} \cdot \vec{a} & \vec{n} \cdot \vec{b} & \vec{n} \cdot \vec{c} \end{vmatrix}$

Because $\det(P \times Q^T) = \det(P) \times \det(Q^T) = \det(P) \times \det(Q)$, the theorem is proven.

Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (G.concept: Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (Gramian-like Determinant)
Product of Two Scalar Triple Products (G.content:
A frequent mistake is losing track of the row and column ordering when mapping the vectors to the final determinant. While the determinant's value is invariant under transposition (meaning swapping the roles of the two sets of vectors yields the same result), scrambling the internal order—such as putting $\vec{l} \cdot \vec{b}$ where $\vec{m} \cdot \vec{a}$ should be—will break the mathematical symmetry and lead to erroneous sign changes or entirely wrong values.

Another conceptual trap: Students sometimes see a $3 \times 3$ determinant and instinctively write cross products inside it. Remember, a determinant must be composed of scalars (real numbers). A dot product evaluates to a scalar, making it valid for matrix entries. A cross product evaluates to a vector. You cannot put vectors inside a standard numerical determinant matrix designed to yield a scalar volume.

Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminou.concept: Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminous Edges
Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminou.content:
Geometry and algebra are intimately entwined in the study of vectors. One of the most beautiful connections is how the algebraic scalar triple product directly calculates geometric volume. 

We establish that the absolute value of the scalar triple product, $|[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]|$, represents the total volume of a parallelepiped formed by $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, and $\vec{c}$ as its adjacent, coterminous edges (edges meeting at a single vertex). 

But what is a tetrahedron? A tetrahedron is a geometric solid with four triangular faces—a triangular pyramid. If we select one vertex of the tetrahedron to be our origin, the three edges radiating outward from that vertex form vectors $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, and $\vec{c}$. How much of the parallelepiped's volume does this tetrahedron occupy? 

Through Cavalieri's Principle and basic 3D geometry, we know that the volume of any pyramid is exactly one-third ($1/3$) of the volume of the prism that encloses it (having the same base area and height). The 'prism' corresponding to our vectors would have a parallelogram base formed by $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$. However, the base of our tetrahedron is only a triangle—which is exactly half ($1/2$) of that parallelogram. 

Therefore, we introduce two scaling factors to transition from a parallelepiped to a tetrahedron: we multiply by $1/2$ because the base is a triangle instead of a parallelogram, and we multiply by $1/3$ because it is a pyramid tapering to a point rather than a uniform prism. Combining these scaling factors ($1/2 \times 1/3$), we deduce that the volume of a tetrahedron is exactly one-sixth ($1/6$) the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the same three vectors. 

This $1/6$ is a non-negotiable geometric constant derived from spatial calculus. Furthermore, because physical volume is inherently positive, but the algebraic scalar triple product can be negative depending on the right-handed or left-handed orientation of the vectors, we must enforce an absolute value.

Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminou.concept: Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminous Edges
Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminou.content:
The volume ($V$) of a tetrahedron whose three coterminous edges (edges originating from a single common vertex) are represented by the vectors $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, and $\vec{c}$ is given by the formula:

$V = \frac{1}{6} |[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]|$

Where:
- $[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]$ is the scalar triple product, algebraically equivalent to $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$.
- $| \dots |$ denotes the absolute value (magnitude) of the resulting scalar, ensuring the physical volume remains strictly non-negative.
- The scalar fraction $\frac{1}{6}$ is the geometric constant mapping parallelepiped volume to tetrahedron volume.

Constraints:
- The vectors $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, and $\vec{c}$ must originate from the same vertex. If the problem provides the position vectors of the four vertices $A, B, C, D$ with respect to the origin, you must first calculate the edge vectors (e.g., $\vec{AB}, \vec{AC}, \vec{AD}$) before applying this formula.

Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminou.concept: Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminous Edges
Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminou.content:
Let us geometrically and algebraically derive the volume of the tetrahedron to rigorously prove the origin of the $1/6$ factor.

Step 1: General Pyramid Volume Formula
The basic geometric formula for the volume $V$ of any pyramid (including a tetrahedron) is:
$V = \frac{1}{3} \times (\text{Base Area}) \times (\text{Height})$

Step 2: Formulate the Base Area
Let the triangular base of the tetrahedron be formed by the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.
The magnitude of the cross product, $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$, gives the area of the full parallelogram spanned by these two vectors. 
Since the base of the tetrahedron is a triangle, its area $A$ is exactly half of the parallelogram:
$\text{Base Area} = \frac{1}{2} |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$

Step 3: Formulate the Height
The height $h$ of the tetrahedron must be measured perpendicular to the base plane. 
The cross product vector $(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$ is geometrically normal (perpendicular) to the base plane. We can define the unit normal vector $\hat{n}$ as:
$\hat{n} = \frac{\vec{a} \times \vec{b}}{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|}$

The height $h$ is simply the projection of the third vector, $\vec{c}$, onto this normal direction. The length of projection is given by the absolute value of the dot product between $\vec{c}$ and the unit normal $\hat{n}$:
$h = |\vec{c} \cdot \hat{n}| = \left| \vec{c} \cdot \frac{\vec{a} \times \vec{b}}{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|} \right|$

Step 4: Combine into the Volume Formula
Now, substitute the Base Area and the Height back into the primary volume equation:
$V = \frac{1}{3} \times \left( \frac{1}{2} |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| \right) \times \left| \vec{c} \cdot \frac{\vec{a} \times \vec{b}}{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|} \right|$

Notice the beautiful cancellation: The magnitude term $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$ in the numerator of the area cancels perfectly with the denominator in the height projection.

$V = \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} \times |\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})|$

Simplifying the fraction and recognizing the scalar triple product:
$V = \frac{1}{6} |[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]|$

This completes the rigorous proof.

Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminou.concept: Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminous Edges
Volume of a Tetrahedron using Coterminou.content:
We have established that $V = \frac{1}{6}|[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]|$ requires coterminous edges. Suppose a JEE examiner tries to trick you by providing the actual position vectors of the four vertices of the tetrahedron, located at points $P, Q, R,$ and $S$ with coordinates relative to the origin $O$. How must you adapt the formula? 

If you simply calculate $[\vec{OP} \, \vec{OQ} \, \vec{OR}]$, what physical volume have you just calculated? 
To find the correct volume of the tetrahedron, how do you mathematically shift your perspective to force one of the vertices to act as the new local origin? Prove to yourself that the volume of the tetrahedron formed by vertices $P, Q, R, S$ can be elegantly written as $\frac{1}{6} |[\vec{PQ} \, \vec{PR} \, \vec{PS}]|$, and verify that no matter which vertex you choose as the local origin, the resulting volume remains absolutely identical.

Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.concept: Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Triple Product
Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.content:
Welcome to one of the most elegant intersections of three-dimensional geometry and vector algebra: determining the volume of a tetrahedron using the scalar triple product. To truly understand this, we must first visualize what a tetrahedron is and how it relates to fundamental 3D vectors. Imagine a triangular pyramid. This shape is called a tetrahedron, meaning it has four triangular faces, six edges, and four vertices. It is the simplest possible 3D polyhedron, often referred to in mathematics as a 3-simplex. Just as a triangle is the simplest 2D polygon built from three non-collinear points, a tetrahedron is built from four non-coplanar points.

Now, how do we systematically measure the space contained inside this shape? In classical geometry, the volume of any pyramid (regardless of its base shape) is universally given by one-third of the product of its base area and its perpendicular height. The magic happens when we translate this classical geometric formula into the language of vectors. Let us anchor our tetrahedron at a specific vertex, let's call it the origin $O$. From this origin, three vectors branch out to reach the other three vertices. These are called 'coterminous edges' because they all terminate (or originate) from a single common point. Let us represent these three branching vectors as $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, and $\vec{c}$. 

The face formed by vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ naturally acts as the flat, triangular base of our pyramid. Vector algebra tells us that the cross product of these two vectors, $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$, is a new vector that points completely perpendicular to this base plane. The magnitude of this cross product gives us the area of the full parallelogram spanned by $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, which implies that exactly half of this magnitude gives us the area of our triangular base.

The remaining task is to find the perpendicular height of the tetrahedron. The third vector, $\vec{c}$, sticks out of the base plane, leaning at some arbitrary angle. The actual height of the pyramid is not the length of $\vec{c}$, but rather the straight vertical drop from the tip of $\vec{c}$ down to the base plane. To find this 'vertical drop', we must project the vector $\vec{c}$ directly onto the normal vector of the base. Since our cross product $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ perfectly acts as this normal vector, projecting $\vec{c}$ onto it using the dot product extracts the exact perpendicular height. 

When we merge the base area calculation and the height projection calculation, the underlying vector operations condense beautifully into the scalar triple product, commonly denoted as the 'box product' $[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]$. Because a tetrahedron takes up a fraction of the full parallelepiped defined by these three vectors (specifically, one-sixth of the total volume), this powerful vector operation provides a direct, highly efficient computational shortcut to find the geometric volume without needing to manually calculate angles or individual perpendicular heights.

Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.concept: Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Triple Product
Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.content:
The volume $V$ of a tetrahedron defined by three coterminous vectors $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, and $\vec{c}$ originating from a common vertex $O$ is given by the formula:

$$V = \frac{1}{6} |[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]|$$

where $[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]$ represents the scalar triple product of the three vectors. This can equivalently be written as:

$$V = \frac{1}{6} |\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})| = \frac{1}{6} |\vec{b} \cdot (\vec{c} \times \vec{a})| = \frac{1}{6} |\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})|$$

Let us explicitly define every component and constraint of this fundamental theorem:
1. **$\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$**: These are position vectors of the vertices $A, B$, and $C$ relative to the chosen origin vertex $O$. They represent the physical edges of the tetrahedron that meet at $O$.
2. **The Absolute Value $|...|$**: The scalar triple product can yield a negative number if the vectors form a 'left-handed' orientation in 3D space. Because physical volume must geometrically be a strictly non-negative real number, we must wrap the scalar triple product in an absolute value function.
3. **The Coefficient $\frac{1}{6}$**: This arises from combining the $\frac{1}{3}$ factor inherent to the volume of a general pyramid and the $\frac{1}{2}$ factor inherent to the area of a triangular base.

**Corollary Form (General Vertices)**:
If you are instead given the coordinates (or position vectors) of four general vertices $A, B, C$, and $D$ anywhere in space, you must first construct three coterminous edge vectors by choosing one vertex as your reference point. For example, if we choose vertex $A$ as the reference, the three edge vectors are $\vec{AB}$, $\vec{AC}$, and $\vec{AD}$. The volume formula then transforms into:

$$V = \frac{1}{6} |[\vec{AB}, \vec{AC}, \vec{AD}]|$$

Algebraically, if the position vectors of $A, B, C, D$ with respect to a global origin are $\vec{r}_A, \vec{r}_B, \vec{r}_C, \vec{r}_D$ respectively, then $\vec{AB} = \vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A$, $\vec{AC} = \vec{r}_C - \vec{r}_A$, and $\vec{AD} = \vec{r}_D - \vec{r}_A$. You would compute these three relative vectors first, array their components into a $3 \times 3$ determinant to find the scalar triple product, take the absolute value of the determinant's result, and finally divide by $6$.

Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.concept: Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Triple Product
Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.content:
Let us systematically prove Theorem 6.38, which states that the volume of a tetrahedron bounded by coterminous vectors $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ is $\frac{1}{6}|[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]|$.

**Step 1: Set up the geometric foundation.**
Consider a tetrahedron with a vertex fixed at the origin $O$. Let the other three vertices be $A, B,$ and $C$. Consequently, the position vectors of these vertices represent the edges originating from $O$. We declare $\vec{OA} = \vec{a}$, $\vec{OB} = \vec{b}$, and $\vec{OC} = \vec{c}$. The base of our tetrahedron is the triangle $\triangle OAB$, and its apex is the point $C$.

**Step 2: State the general volume formula.**
From classical geometry, the volume $V$ of any pyramid is given by:
$$V = \frac{1}{3} \times (\text{Area of the base}) \times (\text{Perpendicular Height})$$

**Step 3: Calculate the area of the base.**
The base is $\triangle OAB$. The area of a triangle formed by two vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is half the magnitude of their cross product. Therefore:
$$\text{Area of base } \triangle OAB = \frac{1}{2} |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$$

**Step 4: Formulate the perpendicular height.**
We need the perpendicular distance from the apex $C$ to the plane containing the base $\triangle OAB$. Let's drop a perpendicular from point $C$ to the plane $OAB$, meeting it at point $N$. The length of this segment, $CN$, is our required height $h$.
To find $h$ using vectors, consider the normal vector to the base plane. By definition, the cross product vector $\vec{n} = \vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ points perfectly perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.
If we draw a line starting from $C$ that is parallel to this normal vector $\vec{n}$, and find the projection of the edge vector $\vec{OC}$ (which is $\vec{c}$) onto this normal vector's direction, the length of that projection will be exactly equal to our perpendicular height $h$.

**Step 5: Apply the vector projection formula.**
The length of the projection of any vector $\vec{u}$ onto another vector $\vec{v}$ is given by $\frac{|\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v}|}{|\vec{v}|}$. 
In our scenario, we are projecting vector $\vec{c}$ onto the normal vector $(\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$.
Thus, the height $h = CN$ is:
$$h = \frac{|\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})|}{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|}$$
Notice we use absolute values in the numerator because height is a strictly positive scalar distance, whereas a dot product can be negative.

**Step 6: Combine components into the volume formula.**
Substitute the expressions for base area (from Step 3) and height (from Step 5) back into the primary volume equation (from Step 2):
$$V = \frac{1}{3} \times \left( \frac{1}{2} |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| \right) \times \left( \frac{|\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})|}{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|} \right)$$

**Step 7: Algebraic simplification.**
Notice that the term $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$, representing the area of the base parallelogram, appears symmetrically in both the numerator (from the base area) and the denominator (from the normal vector normalization). Assuming the base is not degenerate (i.e., $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| \neq 0$), we can gracefully cancel this term out:
$$V = \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{2} \times |\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})|$$
$$V = \frac{1}{6} |\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})|$$
By definition, $\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$ is the scalar triple product, denoted as $[\vec{c}, \vec{a}, \vec{b}]$. Since cyclic permutations of the box product preserve its value and sign ($[\vec{c}, \vec{a}, \vec{b}] = [\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]$), we arrive at the final theorem:
$$V = \frac{1}{6} |[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]|$$
This rigorously confirms that the scalar triple product natively encodes both the spanning area and the perpendicular projection height required to compute the volume.

Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.concept: Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Triple Product
Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.content:
To deeply grasp why the $\frac{1}{6}$ factor appears in the tetrahedron volume formula, we can draw a direct analogy between two-dimensional area scaling and three-dimensional volume scaling. 

Let's start in 2D space. Imagine two vectors, $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, originating from the same point. If we trace lines parallel to these vectors to complete a four-sided shape, we construct a parallelogram. The area of this 'full' 2D shape is precisely $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$. However, if we simply draw a single straight line connecting the tips of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, we slice the parallelogram exactly in half, forming a triangle. The triangle is the simplest possible 2D shape (a 2-simplex) and it occupies exactly $\frac{1}{2}$ the area of its parent parallelogram.

Now, let us upgrade this logic to 3D space. We add a third vector, $\vec{c}$, originating from the same point. If we extrude the 2D parallelogram along the vector $\vec{c}$, we construct a slanted 3D box called a parallelepiped. The volume of this 'full' 3D box is calculated purely by the naked scalar triple product: $|[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]|$. There are no fractional coefficients here. 

But just like we sliced the parallelogram to get a triangle, we want to slice this parallelepiped to extract a tetrahedron (a 3-simplex). How many tetrahedrons of equal volume can fit inside a parallelepiped? Imagine taking the parallelepiped and slicing it diagonally in half, matching the cut that turned the parallelogram into a triangle. You now have two identical triangular prisms. Each of these triangular prisms can be further sliced into three distinct, non-overlapping tetrahedrons of perfectly equal volume. 

If you have 2 prisms, and each contains 3 tetrahedrons, you have a total of $2 \times 3 = 6$ identical tetrahedrons nestled perfectly inside the original parallelepiped! Therefore, geometrically, a single tetrahedron holds exactly one-sixth the volume of the full 3D parallelepiped spanned by the same three vectors. The fractional coefficient $\frac{1}{6}$ is merely the 3D spatial equivalent of the $\frac{1}{2}$ fraction used for 2D triangles.

Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.concept: Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Triple Product
Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.content:
When applying the scalar triple product to find the volume of a tetrahedron, students frequently fall into several severe analytical traps that completely invalidate their solutions. Here are the most critical mistakes to actively guard against during high-stakes exams like JEE Advanced:

**1. Selecting Non-Coterminous Edge Vectors (The 'Path vs Star' Error)**
When given four vertices $A, B, C,$ and $D$, the most fatal mistake is constructing vectors that form a continuous path, such as $\vec{AB}$, $\vec{BC}$, and $\vec{CD}$, and plugging them into the box product $[\vec{AB}, \vec{BC}, \vec{CD}]$. This is conceptually disastrous. The scalar triple product strictly requires vectors that emanate outward from a single, shared origin point (like a star). You MUST designate one vertex as your reference pole. If you choose vertex $B$, your vectors must be $\vec{BA}$, $\vec{BC}$, and $\vec{BD}$. The formula $V = \frac{1}{6} |[\vec{AB}, \vec{AC}, \vec{AD}]|$ only works because all vectors originate at vertex $A$. Using a 'path' of vectors fails to represent the geometrical base and the correctly relative height.

**2. Forgetting the Absolute Value Function**
The scalar triple product is defined as $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$. This operation evaluates the volume as a signed quantity, which is dependent on the 'handedness' of the vector system. If $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ form a left-handed coordinate system, their scalar triple product mathematically evaluates to a negative number. However, the physical volume of a geometric tetrahedron is a strictly positive metric. If you compute $[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}] = -24$ and declare the volume to be $-\frac{24}{6} = -4$, you will lose marks immediately. You must apply the absolute value to enforce positivity: $V = \frac{1}{6} |-24| = 4$.

**3. Mixing up the Dimensional Fractions**
Under pressure, it is easy to conflate the fractional multipliers for different shapes. 
- The volume of a **Parallelepiped** is $1 \times |[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]|$.
- The volume of a **Triangular Prism** is $\frac{1}{2} |[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]|$ (because it's exactly half a parallelepiped).
- The volume of a **Tetrahedron** is $\frac{1}{6} |[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]|$.
Do not accidentally use $\frac{1}{3}$ or $\frac{1}{2}$ for a tetrahedron. Remember that the $\frac{1}{6}$ factor is rigorously derived from multiplying the pyramid formula's $\frac{1}{3}$ with the triangle base formula's $\frac{1}{2}$.

Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.concept: Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Triple Product
Volume of a Tetrahedron via Scalar Tripl.content:
Let us push the conceptual boundaries of the volume formula. We know that the volume of a tetrahedron formed by three coterminous vectors $\vec{a}, \vec{b},$ and $\vec{c}$ is driven by the magnitude of their scalar triple product, $\frac{1}{6}|[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]|$. 

Imagine you physically grab the vector $\vec{c}$ (the vector defining the apex of the tetrahedron) and you begin to smoothly rotate it downward, moving the apex closer and closer to the flat table containing the base vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$. As the apex gets lower, the perpendicular height of the tetrahedron clearly decreases. 

Question: What happens mathematically to the scalar triple product $[\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}]$ at the exact moment the vector $\vec{c}$ is forced to lie completely flat against the table, sitting perfectly inside the same geometric plane as $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$?

Think about the components of the formula. If $\vec{c}$ lies in the plane of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, the perpendicular height of our physical tetrahedron has reached exactly zero. Because the height is zero, the 3D volume of the tetrahedron has entirely vanished; it is now completely squashed into a 2D shape. Algebraically, the cross product $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ produces a normal vector that is perfectly orthogonal to the base plane. If $\vec{c}$ now lives inside that base plane, it must be completely orthogonal to the normal vector. The dot product of two orthogonal vectors is universally zero. Thus, $\vec{c} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) = 0$. 

This reveals a profound mathematical boundary condition deeply tested in competitive exams: four points are coplanar (or three vectors are coplanar) if and only if the scalar triple product of their coterminous vectors is zero. A zero-volume tetrahedron is the definitive proof of coplanarity!

Equation of a Plane via One Point and Tw.concept: Equation of a Plane via One Point and Two Parallel Vectors
Equation of a Plane via One Point and Tw.content:
To build a profound intuition for this concept, we must fundamentally shift our understanding of what defines a flat, two-dimensional surface—a plane—embedded within a three-dimensional continuous vector space. Imagine standing in an endless, empty void. To lay down a perfectly flat, infinitely expanding sheet of glass (our plane), we need an anchor and an orientation. The anchor is simply a known position in space, which we will call point A. This point locks the plane so it cannot freely slide aimlessly through the void. However, an anchor alone is deeply insufficient; a plane can pivot infinitely around a single point, much like a spinning plate balanced on a perfectly sharp needle. To fix its tilt, we need an orientation, which is provided by vectors. 

In this specific geometric setup, the orientation is determined by two separate, distinct non-collinear vectors, let us call them \vec{b} and \vec{c}. These are 'free vectors', meaning they denote direction and magnitude but are not rigidly tied to the origin. The plane is declared to be exactly 'parallel' to these two vectors. If you were to pick up vectors \vec{b} and \vec{c} and place their tails at point A on your glass sheet, they would lie completely flat against the surface. Neither vector would point into the glass or away from it. 

Why must we have two vectors? Because one vector only defines a line. If the plane were parallel to just one vector, it could still spin freely around that vector like a door swinging on a single hinge. By introducing a second vector \vec{c} that points in a fundamentally different direction than \vec{b}, we lock down the 'swing'. The plane is now forced to align itself with the mesh or grid formed by combinations of \vec{b} and \vec{c}. 

The mathematical brilliance of this configuration relies on the concept of orthogonal rejection. If \vec{b} and \vec{c} span the plane, their cross product, \vec{b} \times \vec{c}, generates a completely new vector that shoots perfectly straight out of the plane at a sharp ninety-degree angle. This newly birthed normal vector becomes the ultimate gatekeeper of the plane. For any arbitrary moving point P to legally exist on this plane, the pathway from our anchor A to point P (the vector \vec{AP}) must be completely flat against the surface, meaning it must have zero alignment with the soaring normal vector. This geometric decree of perpendicularity is the raw, intuitive soul of the mathematical equation we are about to derive, perfectly mapping a spatial physical reality to rigorous algebraic constraints.

Equation of a Plane via One Point and Tw.concept: Equation of a Plane via One Point and Two Parallel Vectors
Equation of a Plane via One Point and Tw.content:
The formal theorem establishes the vector equation of a plane that passes through a uniquely specified anchor point A, which possesses the position vector \vec{a}, and remains strictly parallel to two non-zero, non-collinear given vectors \vec{b} and \vec{c}. The rigorous mathematical statement of this plane is given by the equality of two Scalar Triple Products (STPs):

[\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] = [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}]

Let us dissect the profound anatomy of this elegant formula to ensure absolutely zero knowledge loss regarding its components, variables, and strict boundary conditions:

1. \vec{r}: This is the continuous, dynamic position vector of an arbitrary locus point P(x, y, z) that sweeps across the entirety of the plane. It acts as the ultimate variable in our equation. If a specific vector \vec{r} satisfies this equation, the point it points to is a verified resident of the plane.

2. \vec{a}: This acts as the strict positional anchor. It represents the position vector of the known point A(x_1, y_1, z_1) through which the plane physically passes. Unlike \vec{r}, \vec{a} is a static, immutable constant for any given specific plane.

3. \vec{b} and \vec{c}: These are the two constant directional vectors that govern the tilt and spatial orientation of the plane. 

CRITICAL CONSTRAINTS AND BOUNDARY CONDITIONS:
The entire validity of this theorem heavily relies on the strict condition that \vec{b} and \vec{c} must be completely non-collinear. Mathematically, this enforces the rule that \vec{b} \times \vec{c} \neq \vec{0}. If \vec{b} and \vec{c} were strictly parallel or anti-parallel (i.e., scalar multiples of each other, \vec{b} = \lambda\vec{c}), their cross product would instantly collapse into the zero vector. A zero normal vector defines no specific orthogonal direction, causing the equation to degenerate into the trivial identity 0 = 0, leaving the plane completely undefined (it would infinitely pivot around a single line). Furthermore, neither \vec{b} nor \vec{c} can be the zero vector itself.

GEOMETRIC INTERPRETATION:
The expression [\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] mathematically computes the signed volume of a parallelepiped formed by the origin-based vectors \vec{r}, \vec{b}, and \vec{c}. The theorem masterfully declares that as point P (dictated by \vec{r}) wanders infinitely anywhere across the flat expanse of the plane, the generated geometric volume [\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] will never fluctuate; it remains rigidly locked to the constant foundational volume dictated by the anchor point [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}]. This constant volume constraint perfectly sculpts the flat geometry of the plane in 3D space.

Equation of a Plane via One Point and Tw.concept: Equation of a Plane via One Point and Two Parallel Vectors
Equation of a Plane via One Point and Tw.content:
To rigorously derive the equation [\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] = [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}], we must meticulously translate pure spatial geometry into algebraic operations without skipping a single logical step.

Step 1: Establishing Coplanarity
Let point P, having the position vector \vec{r}, be any arbitrary point dwelling on our target plane. We are already given an anchor point A, possessing position vector \vec{a}, that also safely resides on the plane. By the fundamental laws of vector addition, the directed line segment originating at A and terminating at P forms the vector \vec{AP}. Using position vectors relative to an arbitrary origin O, we write this as:
\vec{AP} = \vec{OP} - \vec{OA} = \vec{r} - \vec{a}

Since both A and P lie squarely on the plane, the vector \vec{AP} is fully embedded within the plane.

Step 2: Defining the Normal Vector
We are given that the plane is parallel to the vectors \vec{b} and \vec{c}. By sliding these free vectors so their tails touch point A, they also lie flat within the plane's boundaries. Therefore, the three vectors (\vec{r} - \vec{a}), \vec{b}, and \vec{c} are strictly coplanar. 
To algebraically enforce this coplanarity, we generate a normal vector to the plane. The cross product \vec{b} \times \vec{c} yields a vector \vec{n} that is strictly perpendicular to every single vector lying within or parallel to the plane.

Step 3: The Orthogonality Constraint
Because the vector \vec{AP} lies in the plane, and (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) is strictly perpendicular to the plane, their dot product must inherently be zero. This is the bedrock of our derivation:
\vec{AP} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = 0
Substituting our position vector expression for \vec{AP}:
(\vec{r} - \vec{a}) \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = 0

Step 4: Distributing the Dot Product
The dot product beautifully obeys the distributive law over vector addition/subtraction. Thus, we expand the equation by distributing the normal vector across the parenthesis:
\vec{r} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) - \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = 0

Step 5: Rearranging to the Final Form
We algebraically isolate the variable component to the left-hand side and move the constant component to the right-hand side by adding \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) to both sides:
\vec{r} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})

Step 6: Converting to Scalar Triple Product Notation
By definition, the scalar triple product of three vectors \vec{u}, \vec{v}, \vec{w} is written as [\vec{u} \ \vec{v} \ \vec{w}] = \vec{u} \cdot (\vec{v} \times \vec{w}). Applying this notational elegance to our derived equation directly yields the final textbook theorem:
[\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] = [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}]

Every step here is logically locked, moving gracefully from a physical assertion of coplanarity to a continuous algebraic constraint.

Equation of a Plane via One Point and Tw.concept: Equation of a Plane via One Point and Two Parallel Vectors
Equation of a Plane via One Point and Tw.content:
There are several deeply dangerous pitfalls students stumble into when attempting to apply this concept, primarily stemming from a failure to mentally separate position vectors from direction vectors. 

Trap 1: Confusing Points with Directions
The most catastrophic error occurs when a student assumes \vec{b} and \vec{c} represent coordinates of specific points on the plane rather than free-floating direction vectors. If you are given three points A, B, and C on a plane, and you blindly substitute their position vectors into [\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] = [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}], your resulting equation will be completely wrong. You must first construct the direction vectors by subtracting position vectors (e.g., finding \vec{AB} and \vec{AC}) before applying parallel-vector logic.

Trap 2: Ignoring the Non-Collinearity Boundary Condition
Students frequently attempt to solve for a plane's equation without taking the 5 seconds required to mathematically verify that \vec{b} and \vec{c} are not parallel. If you blindly compute the cross product of two collinear vectors, you generate the zero vector \vec{0}. If you fail to notice this, your equation collapses to 0 = 0. This isn't just an arithmetic error; it represents a fundamental geometric impossibility, as parallel vectors cannot uniquely span a 2D surface.

Trap 3: Order of Operations in the Scalar Triple Product
Another notorious trap lies in the strict cyclic properties of the Scalar Triple Product. A student might write the right-hand side as [\vec{b} \ \vec{a} \ \vec{c}] instead of [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}]. While these look similar, swapping two adjacent vectors in an STP perfectly reverses the sign of the determinant, changing the volume from positive to negative. [\vec{b} \ \vec{a} \ \vec{c}] = -[\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}]. This simple sign error will invert the geometric orientation of your plane, leading to a catastrophic failure in subsequent distance or intersection calculations.

Equation of a Plane via One Point and Tw.concept: Equation of a Plane via One Point and Two Parallel Vectors
Equation of a Plane via One Point and Tw.content:
Let us deeply probe the conceptual underpinnings of this plane equation. Consider the mathematical form we derived: [\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] = [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}]. 

Question 1: Suppose the right-hand side of this equation elegantly collapses to absolute zero, yielding [\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] = 0. What profound geometric truth does this reveal about our anchor point A, and more specifically, about the spatial relationship of the plane to the universal origin (0,0,0)?

Take a moment to carefully trace the logic. The right-hand side is the scalar triple product [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}]. For this volume to be strictly zero while maintaining our constraint that \vec{b} and \vec{c} are non-collinear, the position vector \vec{a} must be perfectly coplanar with the direction vectors \vec{b} and \vec{c}. Because \vec{b} and \vec{c} are implicitly treated as originating from the origin when evaluating an STP, this forces the origin itself to lie squarely inside the plane. Therefore, the equation [\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] = 0 describes a special subclass of planes: vector subspaces that strictly pass through the origin. 

Question 2: What would happen to our conceptual visualization if the vector \vec{a} was entirely parallel to the normal vector (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})? 
If \vec{a} is parallel to the normal, it represents the shortest possible orthogonal distance straight from the origin to the plane. The dot product \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) would maximize its absolute value for a given magnitude of \vec{a}, perfectly equating to the geometric altitude of the parallelepiped multiplied by its base area. By interrogating the edge cases of these vector relationships, we transcend mere memorization and achieve a genuine architectural understanding of 3D mathematical space.

Equation of a Plane via Two Points and O.concept: Equation of a Plane via Two Points and One Parallel Vector
Equation of a Plane via Two Points and O.content:
We now elevate our geometric framework to a slightly different scenario. Imagine you are tasked with constructing a plane, but instead of being handed an anchor point and a full 2D directional grid, you are provided with two distinct anchor points (A and B) and only a single directional orientation vector (\vec{c}). How does this sparse information uniquely lock down a flat infinite surface in space?

The brilliance of this scenario lies in the power of deduction and vector synthesis. A plane intrinsically requires two independent directions to define its 'tilt'. We are formally given only one: the vector \vec{c}. However, the universe of mathematics despises a vacuum, and we can logically forge our missing second direction vector utilizing the two positional anchors we have been gifted. By drawing a straight directed line segment from anchor point A to anchor point B, we artificially manufacture a brand-new vector, \vec{AB}. 

Because both point A and point B reside harmoniously on the flat surface of the plane, the straight path connecting them—the vector \vec{AB}—must be completely trapped within the plane's dimensional boundaries. It acts as an internal spine. Now, observe the grand architecture: we have successfully recovered the missing pieces required for our foundational plane definition. We have an anchor point (we can choose A, though B works equally flawlessly), an internally generated parallel vector (\vec{AB}), and the externally provided parallel vector (\vec{c}). 

By taking the cross product of our manufactured spine \vec{AB} and the external parallel vector \vec{c}, we summon the all-important normal vector that pierces strictly perpendicularly out of the plane. From this conceptual vantage point, any arbitrary point P seeking to join the plane must prove its worth by ensuring the path from A to P is completely flat against the surface, mathematically meaning it has precisely zero projection along our newly summoned normal vector. This visualization bridges the gap between disparate point data and a cohesive, continuous planar surface.

Equation of a Plane via Two Points and O.concept: Equation of a Plane via Two Points and One Parallel Vector
Equation of a Plane via Two Points and O.content:
Theorem 6.40 explicitly dictates the continuous vector equation of a plane that acts as a host to two specified, distinct geometric points A and B (represented mathematically by their position vectors \vec{a} and \vec{b} respectively) while maintaining strict parallelism to a designated non-zero vector \vec{c}. The final synthesized equation manifests as a beautiful equilibrium of three Scalar Triple Products:

[\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] + [\vec{r} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{a}] = [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}]

Let us aggressively decode the anatomy of this equation to extract every drop of its nuance:

1. The Continuous Variable (\vec{r}): This is the sweeping position vector of an arbitrary point P(x, y, z) that evaluates whether it belongs to the plane. 
2. The Positional Constants (\vec{a} and \vec{b}): These represent the rigid spatial coordinates of our two anchors A and B.
3. The Directional Constant (\vec{c}): The solitary orientation vector dictating the tilt along one axis.

STRICT BOUNDARY CONSTRAINTS:
First, point A and point B absolutely must be distinct. If point A perfectly overlapped point B, the position vectors would be identical (\vec{a} = \vec{b}). This would immediately cause the internal spine vector \vec{AB} to catastrophically shrink into the zero vector. A zero vector provides zero directional information, leaving the plane free to spin wildly around vector \vec{c}. 

Second, the artificially constructed spine vector \vec{AB} (algebraically \vec{b} - \vec{a}) must not be parallel or anti-parallel to the external vector \vec{c}. If they are strictly collinear, their cross product (\vec{b} - \vec{a}) \times \vec{c} evaluates to the zero vector \vec{0}. Without a defined normal vector, the unique definition of the plane shatters, and the equation collapses into 0 = 0. Therefore, the mathematical prerequisite is (\vec{b} - \vec{a}) \times \vec{c} \neq \vec{0}.

ALGEBRAIC SYMMETRY:
The left side of the equation showcases a fascinating structural symmetry: [\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] + [\vec{r} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{a}]. Notice the cyclic flow of the vectors. This is not arbitrary; it is the direct algebraic fallout of the distributive laws of the cross product interacting with the cyclic invariance properties of the scalar triple product, cementing a robust framework immune to the arbitrary choice of whether we used A or B as our starting anchor.

Equation of a Plane via Two Points and O.concept: Equation of a Plane via Two Points and One Parallel Vector
Equation of a Plane via Two Points and O.content:
The derivation of this theorem is a magnificent exercise in vector algebra, demanding absolute precision in applying the distributive properties of cross and dot products. We shall not skip a single micro-step.

Step 1: Identifying the Coplanar Vectors
Consider our arbitrary roving point P, represented by position vector \vec{r}. We must lock it to the plane containing points A(\vec{a}) and B(\vec{b}), parallel to vector \vec{c}. 
We first construct two vectors firmly embedded in the plane's surface:
Vector 1: The path from anchor A to roaming point P: \vec{AP} = \vec{r} - \vec{a}
Vector 2: The path connecting our two solid anchors: \vec{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}
We are given the third vector, \vec{c}, which lies parallel to the plane.
Consequently, the vectors \vec{AP}, \vec{AB}, and \vec{c} are strictly coplanar.

Step 2: Enforcing Coplanarity via Orthogonality
Because \vec{AB} and \vec{c} dictate the planar directions, their cross product generates the master normal vector: \vec{n} = \vec{AB} \times \vec{c} = (\vec{b} - \vec{a}) \times \vec{c}.
For vector \vec{AP} to exist within the plane, it must be perfectly perpendicular to this normal vector. Thus, their dot product must evaluate to zero:
\vec{AP} \cdot (\vec{AB} \times \vec{c}) = 0
Substituting the position vectors:
(\vec{r} - \vec{a}) \cdot ((\vec{b} - \vec{a}) \times \vec{c}) = 0

Step 3: Distributing the Cross Product
We meticulously distribute the cross product over the vector subtraction inside the right-hand parenthesis. The cross product obeys distributivity: (\vec{u} + \vec{v}) \times \vec{w} = \vec{u} \times \vec{w} + \vec{v} \times \vec{w}.
Therefore: (\vec{b} - \vec{a}) \times \vec{c} = \vec{b} \times \vec{c} - \vec{a} \times \vec{c}
Our primary equation updates to:
(\vec{r} - \vec{a}) \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c} - \vec{a} \times \vec{c}) = 0

Step 4: Distributing the Dot Product (The 'FOIL' Method for Vectors)
We now aggressively distribute the dot product, multiplying each term in the left parenthesis by each term in the right parenthesis, yielding four distinct scalar triple products:
1. \vec{r} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})
2. -\vec{r} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{c})
3. -\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})
4. +\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{c})
Assembling the expansion:
\vec{r} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) - \vec{r} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{c}) - \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) + \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{c}) = 0

Step 5: Purging the Trivial Terms
Observe the final term: \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{c}). Geometrically, this is the volume of a parallelepiped formed by vectors \vec{a}, \vec{a}, and \vec{c}. Since two defining vectors are absolutely identical, the shape collapses into a 2D plane with strictly zero volume. Mathematically, [\vec{a} \ \vec{a} \ \vec{c}] = 0. The term vanishes completely.

Step 6: Reordering and Resolving Signs
We are left with:
[\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] - [\vec{r} \ \vec{a} \ \vec{c}] - [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] = 0
To match the elegant standard form, we apply the anti-commutative property of the cross product to the second term. Swapping the inner vectors flips the sign of the entire Scalar Triple Product:
-[\vec{r} \ \vec{a} \ \vec{c}] = +[\vec{r} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{a}]
Substituting this cyclic shift back into the equation yields:
[\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] + [\vec{r} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{a}] - [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] = 0

Step 7: Final Arrangement
By forcefully shifting the pure constant term [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] to the right side of the equals sign, we arrive at the immortalized final theorem:
[\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] + [\vec{r} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{a}] = [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}]
The proof is flawlessly complete, devoid of any heuristic shortcuts.

Equation of a Plane via Two Points and O.concept: Equation of a Plane via Two Points and One Parallel Vector
Equation of a Plane via Two Points and O.content:
The algebraic battlefield of this derivation is heavily mined with sign traps and associative errors. Students attempting to reproduce this from memory frequently experience catastrophic failures in the middle stages. 

Trap 1: The Cross-Product Distribution Reversal
When expanding (\vec{b} - \vec{a}) \times \vec{c}, a common and deadly mistake is to write it as \vec{b} \times \vec{c} - \vec{c} \times \vec{a}. Because regular scalar multiplication is commutative, students inherently assume vector multiplication is too. It is absolutely not. The vector \vec{c} is stationed rigidly on the right side of the cross symbol. It must fiercely remain on the right side during distribution: \vec{b} \times \vec{c} - \vec{a} \times \vec{c}. If you accidentally switch the order, you will introduce a rogue negative sign that destroys the final cyclic symmetry, leading to an answer like [\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] - [\vec{r} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{a}], which defines an entirely different, incorrect plane in 3D space.

Trap 2: Ignoring the Subtlety of Cyclic Permutation
The transition from -[\vec{r} \ \vec{a} \ \vec{c}] to +[\vec{r} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{a}] relies on swapping the second and third variables in the STP bracket. Students often memorize the final formula without understanding why the 'a' and 'c' traded places. This leads to them memorizing the formula incorrectly, perhaps guessing the order during an exam. The logic is ironclad: reversing the cross product (\vec{a} \times \vec{c} \rightarrow -(\vec{c} \times \vec{a})) neutralizes the negative sign sitting outside the dot product. Always rely on strict algebraic rules rather than rote visual memorization of the final theorem.

Equation of a Plane via Two Points and O.concept: Equation of a Plane via Two Points and One Parallel Vector
Equation of a Plane via Two Points and O.content:
Let us scrutinize the structural symmetry of the equation we just derived: [\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] + [\vec{r} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{a}] = [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}]. 

Question: The fundamental geometry of a plane does not care whether we subjectively labeled a point 'A' or 'B' as our primary anchor. Our mathematical derivation chose A (\vec{a}) as the baseline, forming the vector \vec{AP} = \vec{r} - \vec{a}. If this equation represents true, unshakeable geometric reality, then using point B (\vec{b}) as our anchor—forming vector \vec{BP} = \vec{r} - \vec{b}—must logically produce the exact same final equation. Can you trace in your mind how the mathematics guarantees this invariance?

If we restart the proof anchored at B, the dot product constraint becomes (\vec{r} - \vec{b}) \cdot ((\vec{a} - \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}) = 0. Notice the normal vector was constructed as \vec{BA} \times \vec{c}. Expanding this monstrous expression will generate four terms. This time, the term \vec{b} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) will vanish into zero because of the duplicated \vec{b} vector. After you rigorously manage the negative signs and meticulously apply the cyclic permutations of the resulting scalar triple products, all terms will miraculously align to reconstruct the exact same sum: [\vec{r} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}] + [\vec{r} \ \vec{c} \ \vec{a}] = [\vec{a} \ \vec{b} \ \vec{c}]. 

This proves that the final algebraic expression has completely absorbed and erased our arbitrary initial human choices, distilling the problem down to pure, invariant geometric truth. Mathematical formulas of this caliber are beautifully ambivalent to the perspectives of the observer.

Equation of a Plane via Three Non-Collin.concept: Equation of a Plane via Three Non-Collinear Points
Equation of a Plane via Three Non-Collin.content:
We arrive at the ultimate and most fundamental geometric genesis of a plane. Ancient Euclidean axioms strictly declare that any three distinct points in space that do not lie on a single straight line will unambiguously and uniquely define a single, flat, two-dimensional plane. Think of a common three-legged stool; it will never wobble on a flat floor, no matter how wildly uneven its legs might be, because the three points of contact instantly carve out a perfect, unique planar surface in space. A four-legged chair wobbles because four points are rarely coplanar, but three points possess an inescapable geometric destiny: they must form a plane.
